utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. May I ask Madam Registrar to please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-02-60-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic, Dragan Obrenovic, Dragan Jokic, and Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Peter McCloskey accompanied by Anne Davis, Stefan Waespi and Janet Stewart, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the parties. For Mr. Obrenovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Michael Karnavas and Suzana Tomanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For Mr. Blagojevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am Mr. Wilson. I am also for Mr. Obrenovic, accompanied by Mr. Slijepcevic, and our interpreter Mr. Karganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I was aware of this confusion, no doubt. Mr. -- For Mr. Jokic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, my name is Miodrag Stojanovic, I am representing the accused Mr. Jokic together with co-counsel Ms. Cynthia Sinatra and Mr. Dragoslav Djukic, our interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And on behalf of Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the accused Mr. Nikolic is represented by myself, Veselin Londrovic, my colleague Mr. Stefan Kirsch, and our interpreter Ms. Lovric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And then I -- may I take the opportunity when addressing the accused in person, may I ask at the same time whether you are following the proceedings in a language you understand, and do you have any problems related to your health? Do you have any problems related to the Detention Unit? May we start in the same order. Please, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand what is being spoken in the courtroom. My health is fine, and I have no problems whatsoever. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for other matters, I don't think there's any point in addressing them at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we didn't hear the beginning of the intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please repeat? There was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I am able to understand what is being said and interpreted into the Serbian language. As for other issues, I don't think that there's any point in bringing them up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So my understanding is that you want to bring up another issue later during this conference; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no point in discussing them because I raised certain issues, but they're still pending. I think the situation is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For my better understanding, you're making reference to the hearing we had immediately following the last Status Conference; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we continue this way, that we will have our Status Conference as scheduled, and at the end, in closed session, a special part relating to the concerns you want to express. No doubt you have the right to express these concerns here during such a Status Conference. Then Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand the language used in the courtroom. I do not have any problems concerning my health. Likewise, I do not have any complaints as to the conditions of detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Only for the record, it should be clarified that Mr. Dragan Jokic has waived his right to attend the Status Conference, as he is currently provisionally released, and the Trial Chamber, in its entirety, has accepted this waiver. Let me give some preliminary remarks. Normally, this meeting already scheduled for yesterday was intended to be the Pre-Trial Conference. Unfortunately, for a number of reasons it was not possible to proceed as planned. It's not only the additional workload emanating from some special events during the last weeks and months, but it's also the fact that the Trial Chamber, and especially the Pre-Trial Judge, was in a situation where under the rules of the ethics of a Judge, a Judge can't act. It is my understanding that pending a motion on disqualification, a Judge can't act. So therefore, and also based on another motion, this Trial Chamber, in its entirety, was blocked for about one month. Therefore, I decided on very short notice that instead of having the Pre-Trial Conference today, this should be conducted immediately before the start of the case, that is, the 5th of May, 2003. At the same time, then we have the advantage that also Mr. Dragan Jokic can be present during this Pre-Trial Conference. The intention is to start with this Pre-Trial Conference open-ended and then immediately to go over to the start of the hearing as such. This, no doubt, is not the best solution, but in the moment, the Trial Chamber is not able to decide on any motions under 92 bis or 94 bis because only an informed Judge can decide on this. This is, at the moment, not the case. Also, this has an advantage. I think it is helpful that the decision on the admissibility of statements or transcripts under 92 bis or expert statements under 94 bis, this decision should be taken by those Judges being the Judges hearing the case. Otherwise, we could have the situation under our rules that the permanent Judges come to different conclusions opposed to those Judges hearing the case. So my first question would be: Are there any principal objections against the idea that in preparation of the case the Ad Litem Judges assigned attend to this case participate in the Pre-Trial Conference to be held the 5th of May following based on the fact that the Secretary-General of the United Nations has assigned these pre-trial -- these Ad Litem Judges already as of the 17th of April to this case? May I hear the submissions. First Prosecution, and then the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now, let's really continue in alphabetical order. Defence for Mr. Blagojevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't have an objection to that, Your Honour. I do, however, wish to raise an issue immediately after this, which I think may need to be discussed before we go into any other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. The Defence for Mr. Obrenovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence for Mr. Jokic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not have any objection as to the participation of Ad Litem Judges even before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And finally, the Defence for Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Nikolic has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that Mr. Karnavas has an issue to raise immediately after this. End of quote. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sometime this afternoon, I think approximately 2.00, 2.15, I received the Bureau's latest decision with respect to my motion for clarification in which the Prosecution joined me, in part, with respect to whether a decision from the Bureau can be -- can be appealed. The decision itself reflects that the Bureau itself cannot make that decision. I think the Prosecutor was correct in pointing out that it is an administrative body as opposed to a judicial body. And in paragraph 5 of the decision, the Bureau indicates that that is a decision for the Trial Chamber to make. Given the -- given Rule 73 and in light of the -- the new -- we were urged to make oral motions, to make sure that I'm fully protecting Mr. Blagojevic's rights and not waiving any, to make sure that I'm acting due diligently, because the Appeals Chamber has indicated that when a counsel fails to act, they waive the issue and they cannot look to the Appeals Chamber to cure the mistakes or the faults of the attorneys, I think it's appropriate for me at this time to ask the Trial Chamber orally for certification to appeal the decision or to seek interlocutory appeal on this issue. The Rules are not clear whether that is possible. If it's the Trial Chamber's decision that the -- that it is not possible, then at least I think the record will be clear that I've exhausted all of my remedies. I've done everything I can possibly do at this point. If, on the other hand, the Trial Chamber believes that I am entitled to file an interlocutory appeal, I would ask for certification. I believe the Rules provide for an oral decision on that. And of course Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. if that were to be granted, then I would file it immediately, perhaps as early as Monday or maybe even as -- I think Monday would probably be the earliest I could get it in. Given the -- given the Prosecution's remarks in its response, in its response to my motion for clarification, it is also clear to me, unless I'm reading it wrong, that the Prosecution is also of the opinion that this is a matter that perhaps should be dealt with prior to trial on a basis of an interlocutory appeal by the Appeals Chamber so at least there's closure on this issue. So in any event, that is my application at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please understand that I will not accept an oral motion on this because in my understanding of the ethics of a Judge, a Judge should never touch a motion on disqualification, and the same is of course true as regards the certification. May I, therefore, please ask you to do this in writing, the request for certification, and, no doubt, I have to discuss it with my colleagues, but then it will be forwarded to the President with the request to assign this to another Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us now come to the questions of disclosure and outstanding motions. We have a number of outstanding motions, especially on 92 bis and 94 bis. I would like to hear some comments from the side of the Prosecution related to the Butler report, be it now under Rule 94 bis or Rule 92 bis (B), and whether the Prosecution seeks under Rule 92 bis the admission of at least some parts of the transcripts in the Krstic case in this case as well in order to avoid overlapping and wasting time with those areas already covered in the Krstic case and then limiting the Trial Chamber to those aspects which are new and of course based on the cross-examination by the Defence. May I hear, please, your observation on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Since this idea was broached yesterday we have considered that, and what we have decided would be that it would be best, I believe, for the overall efficiency of this case to rely on the current reports of Mr. Butler, his narrative and his command report as opposed to his testimony in Krstic. I say that because if we apply the 92 bis Rule for his testimony in Krstic, we would have to withdraw any of the particular testimony that went to the acts or conduct of the accused. And this would be my guess would be a very hotly contested issue, and it would be -- there would be a legal battle throughout the days and days that it took Mr. Butler to testify, and it may cover a large majority of his report since he spoke of many of these defendants in particular, and -- and some of his statements would have affected them peripherally fairly strongly. And I say that because fundamentally, his testimony was outlined and specifically referenced quite thoroughly in his reports which I hope to be part of the record as we offer them into evidence, and I would not intend to have Mr. Butler testify all over again to many of the material that is in those reports, and I would expect that the material that I didn't get to that counsel would object to, they would cross-examine Mr. Butler on and that in the end this would be the most efficient way of dealing with these issues. I think Mr. Butler's two reports, will get done what we need to get done and establish for the record what is best and avoid the potentially contentious 92 bis debate. Now, on the other hand, if counsel wishes not to object to the entry of Mr. Butler's testimony, I have no problem offering it fully, but I am, perhaps, not that optimistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Does any Defence team want to respond on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Gladly, Your Honour. I think Mr. McCloskey is correct that Mr. Butler is going to be a very key witness. His testimony is going to be hotly contested. As far as his prior testimony is concerned, I think in any event, we're going to be making references to it in all likelihood either to refresh his memory or to impeach him. I'm sure that the Prosecution will be doing the same whenever we are attempting to impeach him, and they will probably be trying to bring in portions it have to establish prior consistent testimony or statements. I understand that in another case, in the Brdjanin case, there is a procedure in place that sort of assists the Trial Chamber in limiting or expediting the process where the -- apparently the Prosecution redacts the testimony. They then do have a limited direct, and of course the cross-examination is more or less on the entire event unlimited. It does save some time. I am -- assuming we could adopt something like that, I'm not -- I'm not opposed to it. But with Mr. Butler, he has two reports. I think the Court is going to want to hear Mr. Butler, and I think he's going to need to establish a foundation for his reports. The reports in and of themselves, in our opinion, are not thorough, are not complete, are not accurate, and I think his live testimony is going to be critical. So I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think, then, the answer to this question is already quite clear, and we have to proceed this way. May I then ask the next question I already touched upon. We are aware that there are eight expert reports that were filed pursuant to Rule both 94 bis and Rule 92 bis (B). Why this to a certain extent double filing and double request?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, all our expert reports were filed under 94 to see if Defence would object or not object, and if they don't, then the reports come in. And those experts that we felt did not necessarily go to the acts or conducts of the accused we filed under 92 bis as another means of allowing them into evidence based on, of course, the Trial Chamber's view on the 92 bis ruling. So I think it's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's premature to discuss these submissions in detail. The time limit is, yes, the 31st of March in principle, so let's wait and see what are the comments by the parties. We were looking for an outstanding transcript for Jasna Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we were not aware that we were missing a transcript. This is one of the victim impact witnesses that we were in the process of trying to decide, as we will continue throughout this process, if a witness may be more appropriate as 92 bis. But I did not know we were missing a transcript for that witness. And we are -- with the help of Defence counsel, have identified some logjams in our B/C/S translations and hope and I trust that the resources we are now applying to those lists, we'll clear that logjam within the next seven to 14 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The same seems to be true, that two outstanding statements be translated. This is P185 and P186; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have had a chance to more fully evaluate both those witnesses. In fact, actually speak -- we spoke to one of them and have decided that we will withdraw them from our -- from our list. We at first thought they were going to be critical because of their -- who they were and their position, but after talking to them, it did not appear to be crucial witnesses and so we have withdrawn them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. May I then ask that the outstanding transcript will be in the possession of all the Defence teams no later than next Wednesday. And is it acceptable for all the Defence teams that the Trial Chamber expects the response no later than two weeks after being in the possession of this transcript? Is it okay for you? I can't see no objections. Then I take it as accepted. I was taken by surprise to hear that the Prosecution intends to file two more expert reports, a report from a Mr. Jurien Bijhold. Could you please explain on what this expert should give his expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a Dutch photo identification expert. We have had discussions between Mr. Nikolic's counsel and the Prosecutor regarding particular photos from videos and the people that may or may not have been identified in those photos, and we were unable to resolve -- resolve those identifications. So we have -- several weeks ago we have sent the photo and the video to the local Dutch forensic expert to compare the faces, and we expect -- we've been expecting a report back on that, and we hope to get it next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take it that this expert will not be called in the beginning of the case, that we can live with our deadlines as foreseen under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have had a verbal response to his -- to his conclusions, and they're very neutral conclusions, so I wouldn't expect this witness to be needed to be called at all, but we'll, of course, provide his report to the Defence and we'll see. But my guess is it's not really going to be something helpful for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. A point of major concern, no doubt, is the expectation that we would receive another report from a military expert, a Mr. Patrick Cordingley, and rumours tell me that this report should be fairly extensive. Having sometimes the possibility to watch television, I am aware that this expert is covering, at the moment, the Iraq war. What is your expectation about the time we can realistically expect this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The events in the Gulf have messed up our time frame with Mr. Cordingley, General Cordingley, and we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have been in contact with him this week and are trying to work out a time by which we can immediate with him and get this report going. Though I don't expect it to be the kind of report we're looking at from Mr. Butler. Mr. Cordingley, was a brigade commander in the Gulf and involved in combat that took many prisoners, and he will be giving his basic views of command and control and issues like that, but we don't expect him to be getting into all the minutia that Mr. Butler had gone into. But yes, it is an important report, and we are working diligently to get him and get him focused on the materials from Mr. Butler and the other materials so that he can write his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again bearing in mind the time frames foreseen in the Rules, I take it that this, from your point of view, crucial military expert, will be heard rather to the end than at the beginning of the case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We would expect, as you say, at the end of the case to help wrap up the command issues which would probably be several months down the road. And of course, trying to estimate when that will be is difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I think -- Mr. Wilson, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to be heard on that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: There is a problem here for the Defence. Even if this gentleman testifies some months down the road, one, we need to know what he's going to say because we may also need to find an expert and that expert cannot look at the case until he knows what the Prosecution's expert going to say. So it puts us in a situation of finding people of these qualifications and background is not easy, and so I'm becoming concerned that we're getting so far down the road that if we get this report some months from now and the gentleman's testifying two or three months after that, it really doesn't give us enough time to prepare our case. So I would raise that as a concern on behalf of Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think all Defence teams share the same concern and so does the Trial Chamber. So I think we all should know no later than, say, immediately before Easter, that is the 17th of April, when we can expect. And to assist the Defence teams, a short outline of what this expertise will cover, that we have at least the gist of what will be the area that will be covered by this expert and that this report, in any event, should not arrive later than one month after the start of the hearing as such. I think a final ruling today would be premature. In any event, a final ruling has to take place during the Pre-Trial Conference, that we can come to an agreement. I'm fully aware you have the right to respond and you need additional time to find other experts if you so want in response to this expert, but we come later to the question what is the realistic estimate about the time we need for hearing this entire case. And then based on this, we can come closer to that, what is really necessary for the parties. I fully accept your point. Can we expect that a first outline of that, what we will hear from this expert and what he wants to cover, be submitted to the parties by the 17th of April? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, absolutely. And I certainly would like to get a report within the date you mentioned also. Unless there are some serious difficulties - if he gets drafted we might be in trouble - but I hope he can get the report written and carry on his duties at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. At the moment, I only can state the sooner, the better, and the final ruling will follow then at the beginning of May. We have the Prosecution's motion for order requiring all parties to comply with practice direction on the length of briefs and motion. To be absolutely honest with you, personally I don't like these practice direction because sometimes it may turn out that it's counter-productive when we order a party to limit an important, emphasis on "important," motion or response to a certain page number and by doing so leaving out the necessary quotes, footnotes, and additional material that can be of assistance for the Trial Chamber. But nevertheless, the we all have to obey the Rules, and this includes this practice direction. Therefore, indeed I have to ask all the parties to comply with this practice direction. I hope that the Prosecution can live with this general rule, that the practice direction has to be followed, but in order to avoid unnecessary filings, if there is only, in addition, in case, for example, the practice direction provides for a filing of, say, 20 pages, we have in addition less than more than one full page. No request for leave should be necessary. Can you accept this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. On occasion we get wordy ourselves, and that's -- we would just -- it's asking the leave of the Court that we would -- one of the things we were stressing. And as opposed to putting things single-spaced to try to come within the time frame or various others tricks we lawyers do or things we find ourselves doing. And I put myself in that group also. We are all in the same boat, but, yes, I -- as long as these matters are discussed beforehand, I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And in addition, I would like to emphasise that, no doubt, in case of serious issues than on a case-by-case basis and based on oral requests granting leave for longer motions or responses, we can all live with this practice direction. And in addition, I would really ask, as I put it sometimes, in order to protect our forests not to attach previous filings. I know the underlying reasons, in order to facilitate the reading of a motion that previous motions are attached, but please be aware; we all have our filing system. The Registry has a filing system, and we have immediate access to these previous filings and, therefore, please do not repeat previous filings in the form of an attachment. But may I ask all the Defence teams, could you live with this general practice, that we follow the practice direction without request for leave in case it succeeds no more than to the maximum of one page, because some flexibility should be there? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can live with that, Your Honour. I must say I don't like the directives at all, and I -- I probably am a recidivist, violating them unintentionally. I was not aware that single space was not allowed. It wasn't that I was trying to cheat, although I do have a lot to say, so I do go overboard beyond the page limitation. I would ask that we do away with asking for leave to file a reply. I think I should have the right to automatically reply to a motion that I filed. It keeps the Prosecution honest or the other party honest, because if the other party raises an issue that haven't been raised in the motion, then I have to file leave. Then I have to -- then if leave is granted, then I have to file the reply. It's very time-consuming. And normally what I have to say in the leave is what I say in the reply anyway. So I think if we can have a loose rule of an automatic reply up to five pages and even shorten the time, say, within three days. I could live with that. So I think since we're going to relax the rules a little bit, these are only regulations, directives, we're not exactly ingrained into the Rules of Procedure, we should adopt that as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it complicate the entire process if we would proceed this way that the first paragraph response being no longer than five pages, your request for leave to file the following motion, that it can be done in one motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I did. So you're saying limit the Prosecution or the Defence to a response of five pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was your proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The reply, Your Honour. If I can have five pages of reply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm just discussing reply. Normally you would have, as you correctly pointed out, to file a motion granting leave for reply, and then later on the reply. But wouldn't it be of assistance for all the parties to file in one and the same motion in paragraph 1, the request for leave to file the following reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We could do that as well, Your Honour. Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then for a maximum of five pages and then it would be for the Trial Chamber to decide whether or not to grant leave at the same time, and then we would know what we are deciding about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would be great, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Problems from the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's proceed this way. Then we have a real problem. The number of witnesses. When reading that we have to expect 146 witnesses above them in the moment 90 live witnesses, it's always a shock. Hopefully, but it's of course for the parties to give their assessment on the motions on 92 bis and 94 bis, we can, in fact, reduce the number, and the Trial Chamber will try their very best to review the statements we have got until now in order to find out whether or not it's possible to have even fewer witnesses as live witnesses. But may I ask as to the fact that the Prosecution at the moment is in the preparation of filing updated witness list by the 31st of March, 2003, do you intend to add any more witnesses to this witness list? We heard already that you withdrew two. What about the other side of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. coin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have another we're withdrawing and adding three, so we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Neutral.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- Neutral. And these three are witnesses that just came out of the woodwork, so to speak, most of them, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this new list will clearly identify the 65 ter number of each witness, no doubt. The Office of the Prosecution has indicated that the motion on protective measures will be incomplete, but I think also this would be premature because experience shows that sometimes only on a last-minute basis witnesses are requesting protective measures. Do you intend to file, at this point in time, a special motion on protective measures already, reserving the right to add later on other requests? And course the same will be true for Defence witnesses. But it always is a possibility when the witness arrives and then asks for protective measures that we immediately decide on a last-minute basis. I think this can't -- this is really not foreseeable for both parties in the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That has been my experience, that both parties find this subject to change depending on a lot of things. And we have been able to provide the Defence today with the -- our first 18 witnesses and the order. This is tentative, but it's the witnesses that we're planning on calling and the order, and we're of course -- have people in Bosnia speaking to those people, double-checking to see that they will come here and double-checking to see what kind of protective measures they may want, but it's been my experience that until I have a chance to see the witness before they testify that that could go either way. I, frankly, and it's been my practice in this particular case -- I think different cases have different security problems, but I encourage all witnesses to testify openly, and those that need the protective measures of pseudonym and face distortion, I -- we don't try to talk them out of that. But that is something that largely gets decided many times, I think, in the hotel room as they talk to other people. But as for testifying in closed session, that is something I actively try to dissuade people from doing. I think that makes what we're doing here difficult, both on a practical level and on a larger level. But at this point in time trying to file a substantive motion on this issue is very difficult, and like you say, it's subject to change. But if it really comes down to whether it's pseudonym and face distortion versus open testimony, it shouldn't present great problems either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any objections. I think we should live with this in principle. The next issue seems to be a more sensitive one. That's a question of the OTP's filing, proofing chart. Practice shows that such a proofing chart assisted both the Trial Chamber and the Defence with an overview and probative value of a witness, and for the Defence it's a question of foreseeability. For the Trial Chamber, it's an adequate tool to determine if certain witnesses may provide repetitive testimony. Therefore, based on this, we can ask and even rule that maybe and hopefully a number of witnesses may not be called or it's not necessary to call these witnesses. I know that some Defence counsel are hesitant about this because they are afraid that this could assist only the Trial Chamber, but I do believe, in fact, also based on the experience that it's assisting at the same time, as mentioned before, the Defence. And then this will be true -- the following remarks will be true for the now following points. No doubt, and I think nobody has expressed it in a better and well-put way than Mr. Wilson when touching upon this issue of the question of common law versus civil law when it comes to the admission of evidence. I think that we all are aware that our Rules - and we have to obey the Rules - are predominantly those ones emanating from the common law area, but nevertheless, this is an International Tribunal, and we all are at the same time aware that there are a number of elements emanating from the civil law system. And we should be aware here are acting professional Judges and not a jury. Therefore, from my point of view, there seems to be no obstacle at all to have such a proofing chart, and I invite the teams, the Defence teams for comments on this. From my point of view, it would be of assistance for everybody to have such proofing charts. But before I want to ask or request the OTP to provide these charts, please your comments on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have a brief comment, Your Honour. I did express my reservations with regard to this. I think if it's limited and restricted to presenting some facts, I might not have a problem. If it's argumentative in a sense, that it tends to -- the narration tends to go to persuading the Judge, then I would obviously have a problem with that because in essence it would -- it might, even in spite of the best wishes of the professional Judges, it might tend to at least give them the impression that this is an open and shut case, and it could somehow play a role in the decision-making. So as long as it's based on facts and in a very objective manner and it's not -- we don't have argumentative phrases in there, I don't have a problem. So if they could take out all the adjectives and adverbs, then I guess -- and keep it factual, it will be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You may know that in a civil law system we have an entire file with all adjectives and all adverbs and all the discussion in the trial to -- the attempt to persuade the Judges already before the beginning of the case. Nevertheless, we are acquainted with this, and we know only this, and that what we hear in court is evidence, and the judgement can only be based on this. And we also have learned to forget in case, for example, evidence tendered is, for example, under Rule 95 not admissible. Then we have to forget this. Admittedly for a human being it's sometimes difficult, but as professional Judges, we have this obligation and we know how to do this. Therefore, may I invite the Prosecution to provide the parties and the Trial Chamber with such a proofing chart. Will this be possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. I do need to get a better idea what Mr. Von Hebel meant by "proofing chart," but so far as it seems like a consolidated version of our trial brief and what witness -- the guts of what each witness has to say and where it goes in the indictment, that's not a problem, and I won't be using words like disputatious and other words I enjoy reading in Mr. Karnavas's briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's what would be of real assistance and that we know that a witness will testify to certain charges and without any additional comments, only an a list what can be expected and what will be expected from this witness to have an entire overview, especially when it comes to the question, do we have cumulative evidence or not. I want to discuss in addition to this the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please. Please. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you. Speaking of summaries during the 65 ter meeting, I expressed certain reservation to the effect that the Prosecutor has a number of witnesses who have given four to five statements. The first one, for instance, was given to the security service of the BH army, the second one to the civilian security service, the third one to the AID, the fourth and the fifth one, for instance, to the Office of the Prosecutor. Very often, and I have read a number of such statements, these statements are not consistent, that there are certain discrepancies. For instance, in the first statement, the one which was given after the events, the name of my client is not mentioned, and then it suddenly appears in the last statement. I don't see how the Prosecutor can make a summary of those statements and retain the necessary degree of objectivity. I have nothing against the Prosecutor emphasising certain things in respect of particular statements and drawing our attention to the fact that something was not mentioned in the first statement but was mentioned only in the third or the fourth statement. I would like the Prosecutor to point out to the discrepancies contained in these witness statements. And I am talking about the factual discrepancies. If such summaries can be made, then I will have no objection whatsoever. My previous experience boils down to the following: Out of four statements, the Prosecutor often made a consistent summary. And once we read this summary, it seems to the witness is very consistent and that such would be his testimony. However, if we take into account all previous statements, this turns out not to be the case. We have to be given this opportunity. We have to be -- our attention has to be drawn to all these discrepancies, and the witnesses should be made aware of that. I am aware of the fact that this is -- this can be difficult. However, the experience has taught us that such things have happened. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't more than absolutely agree with your comments, and it's also of utmost importance for the Trial Chamber to have, no doubt, all the statements and all the previous transcripts, at least the hint that the witness has given previously testimony in another case of this Tribunal. But all the statements not included in transcripts should be provided to the parties and to the Trial Chamber, because no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. doubt it's not for the Prosecution, and it should be, first of all, the obligation of the Defence and then later of the Judges to find out these discrepancies, the consistency, and the development of statements. No doubt there will be such a development of a statement. I would be absolutely hesitant and would ask why this is this, if there is a consistent testimony on all single details. Then alarm bells would be ringing. So therefore, I think we are all in agreement that we need all the statements available for the Prosecution, and the same is true later during -- if any -- during Defence case, that the also Defence provides us with all statements and give us at least hints on previous testimonies where transcripts are available. This brings me to already the next point. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. With your permission. While preparing for the Status Conference two days ago we made certain representations concerning this particular issue, and the Defence of Dragan Jokic accepted this proposal, that the Prosecutor should submit this proofing chart, an overview of witnesses and expert witnesses that they intend to call or whose statements would be tendered. Bearing in mind that the Court will base its judgement on the evidence offered in this courtroom during the trial, we believed, and this is still our position, that such a chart is only here for the purposes of helping us and that we should focus when examining witnesses on the facts and how they relate to the individual counts of the indictment. It is certain that the nuances in witness statements, and sometimes even differences in witness statements or what the witness tries to conceal or emphasise in his or her statements will only help all of us to reach the truth through the examination of such witness. We do not think that this proofing chart can contain all of that. And it is our opinion that this chart should contain only basic facts as to when the witness was interviewed, how many times, concerning what particular circumstances, what particular events, and what is proffered through his testimony in relation to individual counts of the indictment. If that is the case, if that should be the case, then the Defence of Dragan Jokic has nothing against this procedure by the Prosecutor. And maybe it would be a good idea to set the deadline for the Prosecutor to do that today, because I think that can also assist us in the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other comments from any other Defence team on this issue? This is not the case. To be quite clear on this, we shouldn't mix up apples and pears. This proofing chart is basically an outline based on the paragraphs of the indictment and telling us, from the point of view of the Prosecution, what a witness allegedly will testify to each paragraph and to each count only. This does not replace the obligation to provide all the Defence teams and the Trial Chamber with the necessary statements and previous transcripts. But my point of concern is based on the experience that sometimes a statement is not updated, and especially in this case, without having had the possibility to go into some details, I expect that the Prosecution will rely in certain cases on statements given prior to the Krstic case. And I'm afraid that sometimes especially related to crucial witnesses it could pose some danger if we wouldn't have updated statements. I emphasise limited to crucial witnesses. Because with a view to the fundamental principle of a fair trial, I'm hesitant whether one can start an examination in chief receiving an updated statement only two days before testimony, sometimes, really, a totally different statement opposed to the statement given, say, four or five years ago. Therefore, I don't expect any concrete answer today, but I would invite the Prosecution to review whether in one or other case it would be appropriate to have already provided by investigators updated statements and especially updated statements especially in relation to the accused in this case, because we are discussing the individual criminal responsibilities of four human beings sitting here in the courtroom during trial. So therefore, would you see a possibility to have these updated statements and then to continue immediately? What about the so-called proffers? Would it be acceptable for you to have these proffers in principle five working days before the witness testifies, but in any event, no longer than two working days before the testimony? I know that we have to balance some interests here. There is of course interest to have the witnesses for as short as possible a period of time in The Hague. On the other hand, I think it's the right for the parties to know in advance what can be expected from the coming witnesses. Please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to make sure I understand, are you suggesting that the material, the guts of the material in this proofing chart be provided to the parties five days prior to the testimony of that witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt immediately. The so-called proofing chart, I would expect that this covers the entire case as it was done by the Prosecution in other cases in the past. I would say to be of real assistance for both the parties and the Trial Chamber no later than 14 days before the start of the case. An absolutely different issue is the question of the statements, transcripts, updated statements, and proffers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I had not heard anything about proffers or updated statements yet, and so that's a new topic for me. And the proofing chart, yes, no problem. Fourteen days before the trial, I hope to get this out before that. So -- because those 14 days are going to be very busy. Updated statements. Most of our statements are either from Krstic witnesses who have testified relatively recently in the Krstic case after providing, like Mr. Londrovic says, unfortunately sometimes many statements. And after going through that process of providing statements and going through the process of Krstic direct and cross-examination, I would think that is fairly fresh and not in real need of updating. Having said that, if in a -- as we speak to our witnesses beforehand, if something significantly is changed or withdrawn, we expect it to be our duty to tell that to the Defence as I think is the general practice here. Proffers, I'm not exactly sure what you meant by that. If you can run that by me one more time, I can think about it and be able to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Usually in the practice of your colleagues, immediately before a witness arriving or immediately after the arrival, there is a document prepared summarising that what will be expected from this witness and to a certain extent sometimes in the form of an update what happened during the proofing phase, when you have new facts or you are aware that a witness will not testify on certain issues and in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would prefer to rely on the summary we provided in the 65 ter filing as well as what will be updated, the short outline in the -- in the proofing notes. And then if something significant comes up, then provide that in an outline form to counsel as opposed to just wrapping in everything that the person might be testifying to in a whole. It seems to be cumulative to me, but new material that's aside or different from the 65 ter summary or the proofing notes I think is appropriate, as I said before. Our 65 ter summaries are not always perfect, but I think your proofing notes will require us to -- to really fine tune those so that they closely reflect much more precisely. Well, we did a good job on our summaries. I think they need to be fine-tuned. The proofing notes will do that. And if there's anything new that comes up, I would certainly provide that in an outline form as opposed to an outline form of what we expect, because really that is what is in the 65 ter summary and in the proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. That's absolutely to the point. When anything changes, when there is new -- seems to be new evidence or other evidence no longer available, this should be provided to the parties and also to the Trial Chamber in advance that we can -- that we all know what we can expect from a witness. And I think related to this, in principle these updated proofing notes, they should arrive five working days before the witness testifies, but in any event, no later than two working days. From my point of view, it's sometimes extremely difficult when we arrive in the morning in the courtroom and then have on our desk a new, updated version of these proofing notes. And this could lead to a situation where the Trial Chamber could come to the conclusion we can't hear this witness today because it's the right of the parties to familiarise with the new situation and adapt to this, especially when preparing the cross. Would this be acceptable for the Defence as well? I can see nodding. Mr. Wilson, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: It would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the other side, I see nodding. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I just wanted to point out, I have many times tried to get Victims and Witnesses to provide me witnesses five days prior to their testimony in order for all of us to be prepared properly, and -- but many times I have failed, and I don't have a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. chance to see that witness, you know, sometimes until the night before or maybe two days before. Though I do expect our statements that we have taken more recently and materially from the Krstic, I don't expect a whole lot of changes. So I think our proofing notes prior to speaking to them immediately before trial should be, you know, as accurate as is practical. But there are found to be those last-minute changes as we manage to finally talk to people right before the trial. And I know you're aware of that problem, because I'm sure you see it every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There have, in anticipation of your comments, I stated in any event, no later than two working days before, because otherwise we would make the reservation from the point of view of the Trial Chamber to reserve the right to say we can hear this witness only one or two days later, depending on the importance of the changes coming in on a last-minute basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just one other thing to add. We will be going into some new territory in this case, and as you have seen, there are quite a few witnesses from the various Bosnian Serb military brigades, and I would, in my past experience, suggest that many of these witnesses would be considered adverse witnesses, perhaps sometimes even hostile, and I would certainly expect that witnesses in this situation may change what they say quite a bit from the time we last talked to them. Maybe not. I don't know. But as I say, it's an uncharted territory. I don't know if they'll speak to me before they testify, but we'll do our best to keep up in that particular experience, because it will be very new and it will be very different than the standard witnesses who we are used to calling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before the break, I think it's not the time to start on the issue of disclosure. Therefore, may I turn immediately to the question of agreed facts. I'm afraid that until now, nothing has changed in this direction, and maybe -- may I please hear the observations from all the parties what about agreed facts and especially on the chapeau elements of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have received some agreed facts from counsel for Mr. Obrenovic and counsel for Mr. Jokic. They should correct me if I'm wrong, but I don't believe there are any significant facts that go to the elements of the case. And I haven't perhaps focused on those agreed facts as much as I could have. Part of that practical reality is it's only half of the Defence counsel that have done that and it still remains very -- a very contested indictment, and the guts of that indictment I'm sure will be contested even by the -- Mr. Wilson and Mr. Stojanovic. So we have all tried. We've all discussed this, and I think what we've come up with is something, by think we do have our work cut out for us at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask in the light of these comments by the Office of the Prosecution is there any realistic chance for the parties to meet with the Prosecution, especially on the question of chapeau elements of the crime? Mr. Wilson, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. McCloskey proceeded on this issue, as I recall, to take the indictment and circle those portions that we could agree to, which we have done. I would always be willing to talk to him about any possible additional things that we might agree to. I have gone over the indictment with Mr. Obrenovic, and what I submitted to Mr. McCloskey represented what Mr. Obrenovic and his counsel felt that we could agree to at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you in addition, what about these extremely time-consuming but of course if it's necessary, it's necessary, the establishment of the chapeau elements of the crime? For example, the existence of an armed conflict at this point in time. Is there a realistic chance that, and no doubt it will only be possible if all the four Defence teams come together and come to a one and only conclusion on these chapeau elements of the crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the circled indictment before me and so I cannot recall, as I stand here, exactly what we have agreed to. We may have agreed there was an armed conflict. I'll ask Mr. McCloskey to remind me if I did or I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I see some nodding on the side from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He did, Your Honour. The armed conflict, according to my trusted authority, Janet Stewart, we do have an agreement on Mr. Wilson for armed conflict. Just perhaps to simplify things, we really don't have any extra witnesses for these things. The witnesses themselves provide that background, so we're not taking up extra court time on witness for these sort of special widespread and systematic, armed conflict, these sort of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, first of all, I think it's up to the Prosecution to prove its entire case. I discussed this matter thoroughly with Mr. Blagojevic. I don't have any instructions on which I can then go back to Mr. McCloskey and say we agree on certain facts or disagree on certain facts. I do agree with Mr. McCloskey on one thing, and that is given the number of witness the that are ultimately -- that ultimately will testify, it really doesn't make much of a difference in the long-run. The case is going to be long. I don't think even if we agreed to any facts it would be any shorter. So -- but I regret to say that we cannot come to any agreement even as to the chapeau elements. I don't think Mr. McCloskey is going to have that difficult a time in producing witnesses at least to present the evidence which he believes will establish those elements. But I'm instruct that had Mr. McCloskey chose to indict Mr. Blagojevic, and so now it's his obligation to demonstrate whether he has the proof, and of course if he does, fine. If he doesn't, then Mr. Blagojevic should be home with his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have invested considerable efforts in trying to comply with this obligation of ours and to reach agreement with the OTP on agreed facts. We have had several meetings. We've tried to take the indictment count by count. But I have to say that progress was very difficult. And we agreed to disagree on key elements of the indictment in relation to our defendant, Mr. Jokic. We agreed to certain points, and in our written submission which we handed in two days ago when we met the OTP, we agreed on some general allegations from the indictment. But as for specific items mentioned in the indictment, we have reached no agreement. We know what we disagree about, and this is quite clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Nikolic is in regular contact with the OTP. We are trying to come to some agreed facts, but whatever one side proposes to the others, the other side rejects. So that we have not managed to agree on anything. The only thing we agree on is that we disagree on everything. I share the standpoint of Mr. Karnavas, my colleague. It's up to the Prosecution to prove what they want to prove. It's up to us to challenge this, and I think we will not be able to agree on any crucial element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clear statement. We know where we are. And we also know that it's time for a break now. Therefore, this hearing stays adjourned until ten minutes to five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to the agreed facts. I think it's only fair that those are brought only to the attention on the consent of those parties to the attention of the Trial Chamber. I think at the moment, we shouldn't know about this, but later on, no doubt, we would need this. Coming back to the question of the first witnesses to be called. I heard that the Prosecution had indicated that already a list has been distributed about the first 18 witnesses. Does this include the estimate of time needed for those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the page. It was just a very informal thing to give them a rough guideline of the witnesses and the order. The times are in the -- are in the pre-trial brief, and a lot of those are Krstic witnesses, and so I hope that that is -- will be as accurate as we can be. So they have, I think, reference to most of these in the 65 ter. There may be a new witness or -- no. I think these are all witnesses they have, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be of assistance if you would have a separate column on the same document listing the realtime estimate, because unfortunately, experience shows that there is a tendency that witnesses stay longer than expected. And we also have to do the scheduling in advance, and the necessary courtroom reservation. Therefore, my immediate next question would be the one: What about cross-examination? Is there any agreement between the parties to have a common cross-examination or separate cross-examination and then by lead counsel or co-counsel? What about this? Mr. Wilson, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did meet on that, all of the Defence attorneys. There is no agreement as to a joint or common Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cross-examination. I think all defendants want to have the opportunity to cross-examine each witness if necessary. In practice, I'm sure there will be many witnesses where perhaps only one or two or even no one cross-examines them, but we certainly want the right to do that. We would suggest that the Court follow the schedule as far as the order of cross-examinations of the defendants as they're named in the indictment, Mr. Blagojevic, Mr. Obrenovic, Mr. Jokic, and Mr. Nikolic. It seems logical and if that's agreeable with the Court, that's what we would do. We certainly think that only one counsel from each time will be conducting a cross-examination. There is one other aspect to the matter of passing cross-examination which we would like to bring to the Court's attention. There may be many instances where when a witness is called, for instance, Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Obrenovic may pass cross-examination because nothing has been said that we feel needs cross-examination. However, as we go on down the list, it's possible that Mr. Jokic or Mr. Nikolic would raise something in their cross-examination which would revise our views on that, and so we would certainly like to have an opportunity to, if we pass cross-examination, that we might revisit that question depending on what comes up afterwards or, for that matter, in redirect by the Prosecution after cross-examination by anyone who has cared to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The first point I think is the most difficult one. From the perspective of fairness, my personal view would be to have a kind of rotating system. For example, starting with the first witness with Defence team Mr. Blagojevic, Mr. Obrenovic, in this order. The second witness starting with Defence team Obrenovic and in this order to allow the parties to start the cross-examination. Sometimes it's really of importance who starts the cross-examination. So therefore, I would appreciate if the Defence teams would come to agreement what is the preference. To do it in alphabetic order or to do it in this rotation system. May I hear your comments on this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: We did not discuss that as a possibility, Your Honour. I'm, as far as Mr. Obrenovic is concerned, we're very flexible. We'll do it anyway the Court and the other Defence attorneys want to do it. We thought doing it in the order of the indictment would be simpler because you'll always remember it. But if you want us to do it that way or backwards, whatever. It really doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's only an option and I want to hear your comments on this. Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I have never been in a case where there was rotating terms. Frankly, I would have to strenuously -- I don't want to say object to that method, but I would take exception to that only in that I think that it should be done on a witness by witness basis. I do not intend to cross-examine a witness unless I have something to cross-examine on, and what we have all agreed on was that we would be meeting with each other in advance of coming before the Tribunal, before the Court, and so we would be able to say, you know, we would know in advance who would take the lead on a particular witness. I would prefer that method, because I think some of us have more interest in cross-examining particular witnesses than others. And so I would respectfully request that you allow us to the extent that we can get along as we are to sort of determine the order of cross-examination. And while I'm on my feet as well, I would like to make sure that we would have the opportunity, I know the Bench is quite active in asking questions and rightly so because they're allowed under the Rules. I certainly would like the opportunity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come to this very critical issue a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear Mr. Stojanovic on this first, please, and then Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when agreeing on how we will use our right to cross-examine witnesses, we decided we should do so in the order that the accused are mentioned in the indictment. However, it is logical that the four Defence teams will not have the same ambitions in relation to each and every witness depending on the nature of the witness's testimony. The Defence of Dragan Jokic has no objections to the Defence teams agreeing before the cross-examination of each witness who will cross-examine and in what order. I think that we will not be cross-examining most of the witnesses who are not directly linked to any of the counts against Mr. Jokic. Your second question as to how we should operate within a team, we have agreed that only one co-counsel will cross-examine, and we shall agree among ourselves who will take each witness in case cross-examination should be necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Londrovic, please, always being the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in principle, the Defence had a meeting, I think two days ago, and in principle, we agreed that cross-examination should be in the order in which the accused are mentioned in the indictment. I have no objection to this, but I support what my colleagues Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Karnavas are said, that is before the cross-examination of each witness, we can agree on the order. I hope we will not be in a situation where we cannot agree, but should such a thing happen, I propose that the order of the accused in the indictment should prevail. One of the co-counsel of each Defence team will cross-examine, and we will agree among ourselves which member of the team it will be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There's an absolute majority in favour of the order, as we can see it, from the indictment, with the reservation that if need may be in a certain case, the Defence teams will tell the Trial Chamber in advance that there will be another order. But we will only accept this on the basis of a unanimous decision by all Defence teams. Otherwise, we will stick to the order as foreseen in the indictment. When I asked the Prosecution about the first 18 witnesses and the realtime estimate, this was on purpose and for the purposes of the planning of the first months. We have to make the necessary reservations for a courtroom as soon as possible, and I have already received the first request for this. The Trial Chamber is in a relatively difficult situation at this point in time. We are in all likelihood concluding the case Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic, but then the judgement has to be written. Opposed - and I think this is not an agreed fact among the Chambers and the Prosecution - opposed to Prosecution, we don't have the necessary staff members to do both, writing a judgement and preparing on a daily basis a case. Therefore, our suggestion would be to start the case on a slow pace. This would, say, three or maximum four days per week. I know that it is extremely difficult for most of Defence counsel commuting from far away or shorter distance to The Hague. Therefore, I invite you for your comments. What would be, from your point of view, the better solution, to make reservation from Tuesday through Thursday, or from Wednesday to Friday, or the third option, from Monday to Wednesday? What would be of more assistance for you? Mr. Wilson, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our meeting with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Sorry. In our meeting with Mr. Von Hebel we discussed this briefly, and it's my understanding that most people, and I speak only for myself at this point, that most of us agreed that Tuesday to Thursday would work well for us. I still feel that way, but I'm not sure that there's a great difference either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That works fine for me, Your Honour, but I'm very flexible. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this respect, we are completely open. You may decide which three consecutive days should be trial days. We feel that the days should not be separated, that they should be consecutive, but we don't mind which days they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have already agreed it should be from Tuesday to Thursday when we had our last conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then let's at least start this way and let's find out whether or not we can speed up later. But before we come to always the most difficult issue of disclosure, let me ask once again, being confronted now with this number of witnesses, this number of experts, what's the realtime, a realistic estimate for the Prosecution? How long do you believe your case will take, including court recess and other foreseeable events?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, my real answer is I really don't know. I would like to shoot for nine months, but I can tell you that I base that on watching the Samac case with this many defendants, just measuring the number of witnesses I know were roughly called in Samac. It's not as many as we're planning but I hope to continue to work to cut Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that witness list down as we resolve our 92 bis issues and see what's cumulative. But I would be very happy to finish the Prosecution's case in six to nine months, but with some 50 plus outstanding 92 bis witnesses and some witnesses that it's unclear whether they will show up or not, it's hard to gauge this very clearly. But I would certainly hope six or nine months but I wouldn't be surprised if it was longer. After a couple of weeks of trial I'll have a better idea. I think we all will, because we'll get a good mix of experts and civilian and soldier witnesses and get an idea of how long cross-examination is going to take. But cross-examination and 92 bis are such question marks right now it's hard for me to give you much more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So even based on optimistic estimate, taking into account that there will be the summer court recess from the 1st of August, then following three weeks, and then the last ten days also in December until -- I don't have the calendar with me at this moment, but I think the first two weeks in January as well, so it would be realistic to state that, if any, Defence case couldn't start before mid-January. Would this be a correct conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's our best, I would say, estimate at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Taking into account that in a case against four accused, the Defence case will take approximately at least the same period of time, then I'm afraid the case would cover the entire period until, say, November. Once again, an optimistic approach. So we have to realise that this case will effectively take, leaving aside for a moment a judgement in case we have a Defence case, then it will cover the entire year 2004. But as you correctly pointed out, I think it's premature. Let's start the case and after the first two or three months see how we can continue. But only for the purposes of the planning of the future in this Tribunal, it is absolutely necessary that we have a clear estimate. We are confronted with the extremely difficult problem, but we only can assign new Ad Litem Judges to another case when the judgement in the previous case has been finalised. If not, we are in this comfortable situation as we are at the moment, that the previous case takes us less than one month and then there is overlapping, writing the judgement in one case and sitting already at the same time in another case. Then following this case, we have to wait before assigning new Ad Litem Judges to another case until the judgement has been finalised, and we have to be aware only that the parties know that the now elected pool of Ad Litem Judges, their mandate expires in June 2005, and the mandate of the now permanent Judges expires the 17th of November, 2005. These are the absolute deadlines for the case. Let's now turn to the issue of disclosure. I'm always optimistic that these problems can be resolved between the parties and only as a really the final arbiter of the Judge should act. May I ask the Defence team for Mr. Blagojevic, are there any other problems than -- that apparently some statements in B/C/S are missing, but I think this shouldn't be a problem, and it could be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With respect to any statements that are missing or that we don't have the translations, as I understand it, we are working closely with -- with the Prosecution, and we have an excellent cooperation on that aspect. Ms. Janet Stewart, I want to single her out for her Herculean efforts to assist us in every possible way. And on very short time notice. So, we're very happy with that. On the global side of it, though, I don't think there is a problem, however, and I don't want to sound like Cassandra, but Your Honour, I had filed a motion requesting that I be entitled to the entire case. You ruled on it. I wasn't clear on it. I filed a motion for clarification but I did submit a letter to the Prosecution, copied everybody including yourself. I am told, I am told that I am receiving everything that I'm entitled to based on your decision. I have no reason to believe that I'm not, and I know that there may come a time when something may pop up inadvertently, but I know that is the exception. I think at the moment I have everything that has been promised to us and has been agreed upon and has been ruled upon in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I was informed that the Obrenovic team is at this point in time missing key statements from the Zvornik Brigade in B/C/S. Has this been resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were missing and I think still at the moment are still missing some statements. It's my understanding that -- we have had conferences with the Prosecutor this week and that those will be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's turn the other way around. Are there any problems to be discussed today for the Nikolic team?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we did have problems with disclosure. Mr. McCloskey didn't believe us when we told him about the amount of documents. However, we held a meeting with Ms. Stewart, and we were able to identify all problems, that is, all statements that we are missing in B/C/S so that we could discuss these statements with our client and prepare for his defence. We were promised that this would be solved quickly. Priorities have been established, and I do believe that the issue will soon be solved. I understand the situation of the Prosecutor. We know that they have a lot of problems with translation, but as we have been promised, I hope that this problem will be overcome in the next few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt, I share your hope. And finally the Jokic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, two days ago we discussed the issue with the Prosecutor while preparing for this Status Conference. It is correct that our team has not been supplied with approximately eight statements of witnesses in B/C/S, but we were given these statements on audiotapes, and we agreed that we should use them for the time being, and we agreed with Ms. Stewart that three transcripts -- three statements of witnesses will be available to us within the next couple of days, next week, the statements which are very important for the preparation of our defence. But let me take this opportunity to raise an issue that was emphasised at the meeting with Mr. Von Hebel, namely the work of the Defence in the context, in the light of the decision of the Chamber on interviews with Prosecution witnesses and interviews with witnesses that the Defence would like to conduct in the field. Pursuant to that decision, it is necessary for the Defence to inform the Prosecutor thereof ten days prior to the actual interview if that witness is on the Prosecutor's list and that the same should apply in case of potential witnesses. We reached an agreement in principle, and I would like you to confirm this today, that when it comes to the first part of this decision, that ten days prior to the interview with the witness we should inform the Prosecutor thereof, that is fine. That can function. As for the potential witnesses, we do not know who they are at this point, and we agreed that we should approach these witnesses, interview them, and then, after that, inform the Prosecutor on that interview, and we -- it is our understanding that the Prosecution does not object to this -- to this process. If that form of work could be applied in the field, that would considerably facilitate the situation of the Defence. We do not wish to cause any difficulties, and if we should encounter anything -- any difficulty, we would of course inform the Prosecutor of those difficulties. As for the witnesses that have already been interviewed by the Prosecutor and proposed as trial witnesses by the Prosecutor, the same applies to those witnesses, including the ones that we have already approached while preparing for the defence of our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Here we are all in agreement. This decision was issued, I think it was, the 18th of February when we didn't know really what the witnesses would be. We have now no later than Monday, this is the 31st of March, the final witness list, and therefore, the word "potential witnesses" can be replaced by proposed witnesses, those witnesses included in the witness list of the Prosecution.
