Can you agree? Sorry, Mr. Wilson was first on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a different problem with the order as it stands and I would like to address the Court on that. There are two problems. One is the ten-day rule and the other is the scope of paragraph 6 of the order, I would respectfully submit and ask the Court to reconsider the rules that we must notify the Prosecution ten days before we want to talk to anyone who has been listed as a witness. It's my understanding that by placing witnesses on a witness list, that doesn't make them the Prosecution's witnesses. They should be witnesses at this trial, and I should be allowed to talk to them. I believe that I have conducted myself appropriately, along with Mr. Slijepcevic and the other members of our team. I can see that in some cases it might be required, based on the experience of the Court, to issue such an order as this requiring a ten-day notice. I don't like to have to tell Mr. McCloskey who I want to talk to. I don't want to seek his permission. I believe that in this instance that there's nothing that's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. happened here that requires anything like that, and so I would like to respectfully request that you reconsider that rule and that we respectfully submit it's unnecessary and I find it demeaning. The other aspect of paragraph 6 which I would respectfully ask the Court to consider is the scope of paragraph 6, because as it is written it prohibits any contact between the friends, relatives, et cetera of the defendants with any friend, relatives, et cetera of people who appear on this witness list. That's a very wide group of people, and the town where my client lives, Zvornik, is a very small town. These folks run into each other all the time. As a precautionary matter, I've expressed to my client's family that they should be very careful and have no contact as you have ordered. But again, I believe that the scope of this order, if the Court looks at it, that you will find that it is very, very broad and it creates a number of problems. I would like to say also there's a practical problem with the ten-day rule for me. When I go to Bosnia, I'm usually approved by the registry to go down there for four or five days. That's all they want to pay for. That's fine. I understand that we have budgets. That means when I'm down there on the first day of my visit and I find out that perhaps I want to talk to another witness or maybe sometimes I get word that witness are willing to talk to me, I can't comply with the ten-day rule because I've got to be out of there by five days because that's all that the registry is authorised me to be there. So there are many practical problems, and I would respectfully ask the Court to reconsider that. And I've talked to Mr. McCloskey about this, and I would be, of course, interested in what he has to say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I give the floor to Mr. McCloskey, please be aware that this is a mutual question. I was just recently confronted with a number of problems emanating from the fact that Prosecution approached Defence witnesses, and it was extremely difficult to settle these problems. Therefore, in principle there should be such a rule, at least to further -- to notify the other side prior to any contact to a witness. Otherwise, this will cause problems. We're in the difficult situation that we have to work with common law rules in a country that has a civil law tradition. And in a civil law tradition, it would be against all rules of ethics to contact any witness before trial. The first opportunity to contact in a civil law country is in the courtroom. Therefore, from the perspective of people living in former Yugoslavia, for them it's a really shock sometimes to be approached by Defence counsel or having been here as Defence witness, then being immediately afterwards approached by the Prosecution whether they would be ready to testify as Prosecution witness in other cases. And we really have to be aware that this is an extremely serious problem, because more and more we should be aware that all the cases we are hearing here are only slices of one huge case, and a witness testifying on behalf or called by the Defence can maybe necessarily be asked by the Prosecution the next day, "Are you prepared in the other direction to testify as Prosecution witness?" These problems will, I think, become more and more predominant, and therefore, we have to have some rules. But I invite Mr. McCloskey. What are your comments on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do think the rule is an appropriate rule, especially as we look towards some of the more vulnerable and perhaps fearful people on our witness list given the context of not only the civil law system but the war and the situation they find themselves in. Having said that, however, I think that perhaps in discussion was Defence counsel we may be able to resolve the problem, because I think it's a more limited problem than we may -- than I'm actually comfortable with talking about in open court. But I think if Defence counsel and I get together we may be able to resolve this. It might not be exactly to the order of your rule, but I think we can get back to Mr. Von Hebel, and I think we can both satisfy the spirit of that rule and the concerns of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this ten-day rule is a guideline, not more, not less. And if the parties come to an agreement that without this notice of ten days based on the assessment of the Prosecution, there's nothing prohibiting Defence counsel to act without this ten-day rule. It's a guideline. And in case you come to an agreement that you mention correctly, unfortunately the Registrar can only pay for four or five days, maximum a week, of a visit, that you can come to an agreement that these witnesses be heard. And in case Prosecution comes to the conclusion this is a special, vulnerable witness, please take into account this ten-day rule or let us please prepare the witness that -- and in essence it comes down to this problem that the Prosecution has the possibility to tell a witness in advance, "You should know you will be approached by Defence counsel. Please don't be afraid." This is that what the rules tell us, and we have to obey the rules. And this will also assist you when approaching witnesses, I would say. This is the best solution, and this ruling, especially under paragraph 6, should be handled and implemented in this -- with this flexible approach. I think when we do this, everybody could live with this. I can't see any objections. Then let's proceed this way and regard the ten days as a guideline. In case parties agree, then it's not mandatory. Now the other way around. Any complaints by the Prosecution regarding reciprocal disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we would like reciprocal discovery, disclosure at the earliest possible time so we can work on our case and be prepared to properly put on our case. The rules are somewhat vague about timing related to Defence materials, but I think as the Defence becomes clear about -- especially about documents, what documents they may want to use as exhibits, that would be especially appreciated, because I think clearly when the Defence does come across important documents that are not part of the collection of the Prosecution that they know that's something they will want to be using. And so that's all I would have to say on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have to take into account that it's extremely difficult for especially the Defence in this case. You said "When you come across a document that should be disclosed to the other side based on this reciprocal disclosure." With this deluge of paperwork, I don't think that one party deliberately will not live up to the obligations under this rule, and the same is true but to a lesser extent because the Prosecution has the possibility of this huge database, and therefore, I don't believe that at this moment there has to be any ruling on the question of this kind of disclosure. I think the parties will do their very best when they come across such a document and then immediately to disclose this. Coming back to the opening of the case. I heard from Mr. Von Hebel that the Prosecution estimates that the opening statement will take two to three hours. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question was what about statements for the Defence? For me, this is a very serious issue. From my point of view, the fact that an accused has chosen not to defend himself but make use of Defence counsel does not at the same time automatically waive the right to make own statements. Under our rules, it's foreseen, as we all know, that an accused may give testimony as a witness. Typical common law solution, unheard in a civil law case. In addition, this is the possibility of an 84 bis statement. Furthermore, following the approach in Kunarac Appeals Chamber, the accused enjoys, no doubt, the right of having the last word if he so wants under the guidance of Defence counsel. But nevertheless, in my opinion, under the guidance of professional Defence counsel, it is the right of an accused, whenever he wants, and the Trial Chamber feels this would be an appropriate time to hear an accused on this, to make a statement or to give a statement under the rule 84 bis applied in analogy. This means there can't be any question, and the Trial Chamber has to rule on the probative value of this statement. Are there any principal objections by the parties to this approach? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, first of all, let me reassure you that I am -- I fully agree with your interpretation of the rules, and I fully agree with you that it is the right of the accused, and I support that right, and I think that at least with respect to Mr. Blagojevic, I anticipate that he will be making a statement at the beginning of the proceedings which would be in addition to opening statement by counsel. So I understand the rules. I understand how they come about, and I think we wish to avail ourselves of the opportunity provided in the rules, which I think is an excellent rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I take it that we can expect that instead of this form of opening statement your client would be -- Defence team would like to have in addition a response to the OTP statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here is what I would like, Your Honour: The client obviously -- Mr. Blagojevic is entitled to make his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. That's one issue. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is one issue. Now -- this is going to be a long trial. I think the Prosecutor was extremely optimistic. Probably may take close to a year before they finish their case. Mr. McCloskey is a trained lawyer. He's going to get up and in three hours or more or less put -- give you a picture of what he believes the evidence will show in this particular case. It's his opportunity to showcase his case and of course begin the persuasion process even though opening statements, we all agree, is not evidence. Nonetheless, statistics have shown that it can be very persuasive. I would like to have the opportunity to be able to give a short rebuttal at that point, say 30 minutes to 45 maximum. I don't think I will need that entire time, but I would like to be able to give you also an opportunity to immediately hear our rebuttal to that opening. Because of the magnitude of this particular case or any case before this particular Tribunal, and because we have this hybrid system, it's impossible for a Defence, no matter how prepared they are, to give a 100 per cent opening at the conclusion of the Prosecution's opening. Therefore, we would also like to be able to give an opening statement, a full opening statement, at the conclusion of the Prosecution's case because perhaps on some counts, maybe even all counts, they will not be able to prevail on a motion for judgement of acquittal which will follow the presentation of their case in chief. Of course, we want to being fair to the Prosecution, and they have indicated, they have expressed a willingness to go along with our proposal provide that would they have that opportunity, in other words, to present a small rebuttal at the conclusion of our opening statement which will begin at the opening of our case in chief or our case. And I have no problem with that. I think that's fair. But I think that it won't take that much time. We're talking about a limited amount of time. I think that given the nature of this case, we would like to be able to share with you our thoughts and how we believe the evidence will turn out as early as the Prosecution's case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt this will -- would assist the Trial Chamber, because, yes, hearing the first statement by the Defence only maybe nine months or one year later would facilitate, and it may serve as an eye-opener for the Trial Chamber if we can have your views at the beginning of the case, of course for a limited period of time. But this rule, no doubt, should be applied mutually. Therefore, this would mean that after the start of the Defence case, the Prosecution would enjoy the right also to have a short, let's call it, rebuttal or response to your opening statements. Are there any objections by the Prosecution to this point, leaving aside the point of own statements given by the accused in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I would be interested to hear what other Defence counsel have to say on this point. I am open to innovations, but the rules lay out the traditional approach, and my concern is that the rebuttal will turn into argument, both on the Defence counsel and perhaps from the Prosecution. And perhaps this is a little bit too much lawyering going on. Though, I think it's an interesting idea and I'm not dead against it, but I would like to hear other counsel's feelings on it so that we might go into this with some perhaps agreement, because it is interesting. It's an idea that Mr. Karnavas brought up, and he has now acknowledged no objection to the Prosecution response. So I would like to hear what other Defence counsel have to say about it. I would not want to commit myself right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, like Mr. McCloskey, I think it is also an interesting idea. I'd like to think about it some more. I think I like all parts of it except the government's rebuttal to our opening. So I would like to think through that briefly before I take a position on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think there's time enough, and we can decide on this issue maybe the 5th of May. But let's first hear the other submissions. Mr. Stojanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We analysed this issue in the context of Rule 84 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and I feel that we are now in a new situation. As for Dragan Jokic's Defence team, we said so the day before yesterday; if the OTP and the Defence of an accused agree that after the opening statement by the OTP, which is expected to last three hours, the Defence of Blagojevic is able to take half an hour to present the main lines of defence, in that case, the Defence of Dragan Jokic would also request that we be allowed half an hour to put forward the main points of his defence, taking into account all that we have to say in connection with the allegations against him. After the Defence case, the OTP would also have the right to rebut the opening statement of the Defence in the same way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And Mr. Londrovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of the accused Nikolic discussed this issue with our client, and we reached the conclusion that the rule should be respected. The Prosecutor has the right to an opening statement, and the Defence has to decide whether to make their opening statement after the OTP opening statement or at the start of the Defence case. We considered what response we could make to the OTP immediately after the opening statement, not knowing what it will be, but assuming that it will be what is stated in the pre-trial brief to which we have responded, today we decided that whatever Your Honour decides, we shall have our opening statement at the start of the Defence case. But we have no objection to the other Defence teams being given the opportunity to present their arguments briefly as they proposed. We do not challenge their right to this, but today we reached our decision, and we shall have our opening statement at the start of our Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clear decision, but I think it would be only fair to reserve your right to also present an opening statement when the Defence case starts. So I think it shouldn't be an either/or. In some cases there is a development throughout the case that would bring you in a situation that it would be appropriate to hear additional remarks immediately when your case will start. But I share the view of Mr. Wilson. We should think about this again. We had a final decision by Mr. Londrovic, and let's revisit this question when the time is ripe for this, and please let us know what you are planning no later than the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. Just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My only concern if it comes -- obviously if I'm going to do -- if -- if the Court would allow for us to make a short presentation, it takes a lot more time to prepare a cogent statement than to just get up and speak for hours and hours. Obviously I don't intend to make an argument. I know the difference between opening statement and closing argument. But we would like to have some, perhaps even a what week earlier a notice, because it will take a considerable amount of time to put a cogent 30-minute opening statement for -- that would be relevant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think also here it's premature to rule finally. We take into account your observation. May I ask, are there any other issues to be discussed already today save the one point -- sorry, I forgot to ask the Prosecution. Does the Prosecution agree in this case that it is the right to address the Trial Chamber that the accused tried to address the accused -- the Trial Chamber following Rule 84 bis, not only at that point in time foreseen under the Rules but also in addition when an accused, having heard the advice of Defence counsel, wants to take the floor and to address the Trial Chamber by a statement. Would you have any principal problems with this approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, my problems with that approach would be much less so if I was able to question the accused after his statement, but that perhaps goes back to my fundamental background in that statements don't come in without questions from the parties. I understand this is certainly different. The rules are different. But as we get away from the established rule and move into a more fluid approach, I think we could also consider perhaps a point where the Prosecution could enter into this also, or perhaps direct questions to the Court to ask the accused. Given our knowledge of the case and that certain things may come out, questions that are burning to be asked could not be asked under the current Rules as I understand them. So in principle I am interested in the ongoing approach a bit away from the Rule, but I would just ask to perhaps if we do get away from the Rule as it's written, we may consider approaches that would take my concerns into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that there are no principle objections, and let's find out. It may turn out that the -- that Defence counsel believe it's more appropriate that the accused makes use of the right to remain silent. So let us wait and see. But in principle, I see this as a human right. In principle, I regard it as a fundamental right of an accused not to be the mere object of a criminal procedure but an active participant being subject of the proceedings. Let's not discuss theoretical questions. Are there any practical questions in the moment for today? I don't want finally to discuss the guidelines for the admissibility of evidence. I have to thank the parties for their comments. I already now can tell you that some of them will be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. taken into account. Let me only give one comment on this. I think we should make a clear distinction between, on the one-hand side, the admission into evidence and, on the other side, the burden of proof. I think there is no rule or guideline necessary. The burden of proof is with the Prosecution. And also the test is quite clear. Therefore, the question of the weight of a document or evidence should not be discussed in-depth during the admission of evidence. No doubt the test is proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and therefore, this should not form part of these guidelines. All the other comments will be seriously taken into account and, no doubt, some parts have a number of merits. And as I also addressed Mr. Wilson previously, we are aware that we are in a predominantly common law system, and it is not for the Trial Chamber to say: Fill the gaps where the Prosecution may have failed to prove their case. This is not the point. It might also be that we feel it necessary to hear additional evidence not knowing at all in advance what the outcome will be. As experience shows, sometimes a Chamber witness serves more the interest of the Defence; sometimes it serves more the interest of the Prosecution. So the Rules provide under Rule 98, but quite clearly this is the exception, not the rule. As regards the questioning by the Judges, the Rules provide, no doubt, that at any point in time we are allowed to put questions to witnesses. Sometimes in order to streamline the case; sometimes in order not to come back to a document which is already on the ELMO. And there are a number of reasons why for especially technical problems we will put these questions. But as I emphasised already earlier and you can read it in the guidelines, in principle, we should be aware that no doubt we are a criminal Tribunal, and the first criterion is the question of relevance. And I would appreciate that the question of relevance would already be taken into account at an earlier stage. That would minimise the disclosed paper. But it's my belief that as to the fact that we are mandated under chapter VII of the charter of the United Nations, we can't accept to live with the virtual reality. In this case, in the moment, I can't see any such danger that we will confront it by agreed facts that have nothing to do with real facts. I don't know whether you are aware that the rules on the ICC are slightly different on this issue, giving the Judges a little bit more leeway. But in the concrete case, we will show, no doubt, the necessary self-restraint, but on other hand, when we regard it as mandatory, to clarify a core issue of the case, then we will not hesitate to call a witness, to put additional questions to a witness, but as mentioned, this will be the exception, of course, not the rule. The burden of proof is with the Prosecution. We have the Rule 90, what is the burden of the Defence. I think maybe in this case it's even more limited than in other case what the Judges have to do proprio motu, but we have to always be aware of our obligations explicitly mentioned and stated in the Kupreskic appeal judgement, even in case when both parties don't want to hear a witness, it might be the obligation for the Chamber to hear an additional witness. And therefore, this has also to be taken into account. I think in the moment it's a more theoretical problem than a practical one. Be assured that we follow the principle that this is a predominantly common law system. Any other issues to be raised in the moment? Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, Mr. President. Mr. Von Hebel mentioned, it was almost in passing, views on legal motions and mentioned your viewpoint about oral motions, and I wondered if you could clarify what your expectations are regarding the filing of legal motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From my point of view, in principle all motions should be oral motions in order to avoid, as I like to say, unnecessary filings. When we are here together, in principle oral motions should be the rule, and an oral response also the rule. In case of serious, especially legal problems, then on a case-by-case basis, the Trial Chamber would invite the parties to submit their view in writing. But in principle, it should be an oral hearing also related to these legal issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could be heard just on that point. As the Court probably is aware, I file occasionally motions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We're aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do so sparingly, but nonetheless I do so when I think it's necessary to make a record, only because I want to make sure of two things one, that I am diligent in protecting Mr. Blagojevic's rights, but also I think it's always a good idea for the lawyer to put himself on the line in the event the case has to be on appeal where another lawyer might look at the record and suggest that the accused was not properly served by his own lawyer. So those are the two reasons why I file motions. One, to protect his record, but also to give him the opportunity at the conclusion of the trial, if we have to be on appeal, for him to have the basis, if it's there, to raise an ineffective assistance of counsel. I fully support the -- your suggestion of having oral motions. There may come a time, however, Your Honour, where you make a ruling with which, with all due respect, I might disagree. Or I may feel perhaps because of the shortness of time I have not been -- I have not had the opportunity to properly address the issue, so it's always been my belief and my practice to then file a supplemental to the record to make sure that whatever it was that I was trying to convey is conveyed properly. So I -- and I would like to make sure that I would be given that opportunity. I can understand the Prosecutor wanting to have oral motions. I can understand His Honour feeling that that's the best approach. But sometimes motions have to be filed in writing to make sure that we have a clear record, and of course the decision sometimes I think needs to be in writing as well so we all have guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely, and nobody can prohibit you from filing written motions. And as I mentioned beforehand, it may even be the case that especially on legal issues we would ask the parties to submit written motions because here we have to be extremely careful with the wording. And this is true not only for the parties but also for the Chamber. Therefore, it should be decided on a case-by-case basis, but in principle, I believe oral rulings will save a lot of time, a lot of money, and protecting a lot of our forests. Any other issues? Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we filed a motion requesting an extension by a week of the deadline for our response under Rules 92 and 94 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It was only in early March that I received both the Prosecution motions with their many addenda, and together with my co-counsel, I looked through all of these documents. However, our deadline is the 31st, but we shall lose some time travelling now, and I have heard that my colleagues from the Obrenovic Defence have been granted an extension until the 7th of April. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid a written decision is already filed. I don't know whether it's been distributed or not. The Trial Chamber came to the conclusion that the reasons justifying the extension for the one Defence team are not on the same level as your submission alludes to and that there is a clear factual distinction between made, and therefore, at this point in time, we didn't feel that there would be a justification for an extension of one week. Any other issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would seek clarification on one point. If I understood you correctly, you said that by the 31st of March, the Prosecution would submit a final list of their witnesses. Am I correct in saying that after this list is submitted there will be no further potential witnesses of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have already redacted the word "potential" witnesses and we called it now "proposed" witnesses. No doubt that at any point in time both parties can request, if it's in the interest of justice, to amend the witness list or to replace the one or other witness for unforeseen reasons not available. This is, of course, true for both parties. I can't see any other requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I have one request, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: On the Prosecution's notice of compliant with Rule 66(A)(ii) under their disclosure obligations, paragraph 6 talks about the fact that they intend to update the expert witnesses from the Krstic trial. I just want a clarification on when we have the deadline for these updated expert witness reports, because it wouldn't fit under the same ruling that the court just gave for the five maximum, minimum two-day notice for the witnesses and we really need to be prepared for the updated version which would be the relevant part to the Zvornik Brigade, I would imagine, as soon as possible. Could we possibly have a deadline for the updated expert witness reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there -- that fits into roughly two categories as I recollect. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I think the Christian Easter is an appropriate date. The parties could use these holidays for reading the additional information. So would it be appropriate to give a time limit of the 17th of April also in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That would be fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can live with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. So there is no misunderstanding, immediately after this hearing, we will have in closed session, as requested by Mr. Blagojevic, an additional conference.
